To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
repeated cocaine, morphine and stress increase GluR1 expression in the ventral Tegmental area, a brain region containing mesolimboc dopamine neurons.
repeated treatment with drugs of abuse (cocaine, morphine) and stress (restraint) increased the expression of AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptor subtypes in the VTA of the rat brain.

chronic cocaine and stress treatments increase the expression of AMPA receptor subunits (GluR1) and NMDA receptor (NMDAR1) subunits in the VTA, whereas other drugs of abuse that lack sensitizing or reinforcing properties have no effect on these proteins.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the long-term neurochemical and neuroanatomical adaptations of the mesolimibic dopamine system that are induced by chronic cocaine treatment.
the molecular mechanisms underlying the long-term effects on brain function of drugs of abuse and other stressors, and the common and cross-sensitivity of their actions on brain function.
understanding how repeated exposure to drugs of abuse alters brain function.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
repeated cocaine treatment increases the expression of the GluR1 AMPA receptor and NMDAR-1 NMDA receptor proteins in the VTA of rat brain.
chronic cocaine administration increased the expression of AMPA and NMDA glutamate receptors in the rat ventromedial tegmental area, a nucleus containing mesocortical and mesolimbic dopamine neurons.

the regulation of GluR 1 and NMDA 1 in the ventral mesencephalic area is a result of a common mechanism of drugs of abuse and stressful stimuli, and this regulation may represent an important cellular mechanism by which these stimuli affect mesolimbic dopamine function.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

repeated exposure to drugs of abuse or stress can alter the expression of specific glutamate receptor subtypes in the VTA, and that this change in receptor expression may be a common mechanism underlying the long-term effects that these agents exert on mesolimbocortical DA function.

the repeated exposure to drugs of abuse and stressful stimuli increases the expression of Glutamate Receptor subunits in the VTA, which could lead to long-term changes in the mesolimbocortical DA pathways.

drugs of abuse and other stressors that can elicit cross-sensitization effects on DA function in the nucleus accumbens (NAc) and VTA can also alter the expression of glutamate receptor subtypes in the VTA that are implicated in the regulation of DA function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
drugs of abuse can increase the expression of AMPA and NMDA receptors in the ventral midbrain, which may contribute to their ability to alter the function of dopamine neurons.

the repeated use of drugs of abuse can alter the function of the glutamate receptors in brain regions that are involved in drug reward and addiction, and that these changes are similar to the changes induced by stress.

drugs of abuse, stress, and other psychotropic compounds can alter glutamate receptor sub-unit levels in the VTEA, but the changes in subunit levels are not necessarily related to the reinforcing and/or cross-sensitization properties of the compounds.
